chunks.title: Ask the tutor | Maker by Curiosta
chunks.heading: What to expect
chunks.text: Answers come from an AI model reading pages on this site. It can be wrong, so check anything important on fabacademy.org . It will not do your assignments for you. It coaches, explains and reviews. This site has no server and stores nothing about you. Your questions go from your browser to OpenRouter and the model provider you pick, under their terms and privacy policies. Where something is not covered on the official Fab Academy pages or on this site, the tutor should say so rather than guess.

chunks.heading: Learning outcomes
chunks.text: Identify the advantages and limitations of 3D printing. Apply design methods and production processes to show you understand 3D printing. Demonstrate how scanning can digitize objects.

chunks.title: Module 6: 3D scanning and printing | Fab Academy companion | Maker by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Clarified in the official FAQ
chunks.text: 'Not easily made subtractively' means features such as undercuts, overhangs, print-in-place or nested parts that cannot be taken apart. You do not need to include the scan file, which can be very large; screenshots of the process and result are fine. Cleaning up the scan is not required, but it is useful to learn. All modules also follow the general essentials (original files in your archive, compressed media, acknowledgements, AI prompts documented) and the commercial board policy . Summary of both .

chunks.title: Module 6: 3D scanning and printing | Fab Academy companion | Maker by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Documentation checklist
chunks.text: The official "have you answered these questions?" list for this module, paraphrased. Tick each one off in your documentation. Linked to the group assignment page. Explained what you learned from testing the 3D printers. Documented how you designed and printed your object, and why it could not easily be made subtractively. Documented how you scanned an object. Included your original design files for printing. Included your hero shots.

chunks.title: Module 6: 3D scanning and printing | Fab Academy companion | Maker by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Bare-minimum vs exceptional
chunks.text: Author's interpretation Author's interpretation, not official Fab Academy grading. Use it to aim your work and check your documentation, and confirm what counts with your instructor.

chunks.title: Module 6: 3D scanning and printing | Fab Academy companion | Maker by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Bare-minimum
chunks.text: Group work: a test print that checks design rules for your printer (for example clearances, overhangs, bridges, thin walls or tolerances), with the slicer settings, photos, measured results and the rules you will now follow. An object that could not be made subtractively (for example internal cavities or interlocking moving parts), with CAD files, slicer settings and photos of the print. A written argument for why the object cannot be made subtractively. A 3D scan of an object: the method you used, the resulting mesh, and any problems you hit. Printing the scan is optional in the assignment; if you skip it, say so.

chunks.title: Module 6: 3D scanning and printing | Fab Academy companion | Maker by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Exceptional
chunks.text: The group test results are visibly used in your own design (for example a clearance you measured), not just reported. Print preparation is deliberate: orientation and support choices compared, with photos of the outcomes, including failed prints and what you changed. The scan is cleaned up (mesh repair), checked against real measurements of the object, and printed. Parametric or editable CAD in open or widely readable formats, so others can modify it. A link to your final project: where this part or technique will be used. Ask the tutor about this module Coming back after a break?

chunks.title: Module 6: 3D scanning and printing | Fab Academy companion | Maker by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Common pitfalls
chunks.text: The author's notes, partly drawn from the official FAQ. Not official grading. A shape that a mill could make just as well, such as a simple box or extrusion. Reporting group test results without using them in your own design. No slicer settings recorded. Scanning a shiny or featureless object and giving up; matte spray or added texture often helps photogrammetry.

chunks.text: PrusaSlicer open slicer UltiMaker Cura open slicer Prusa guide to supports support settings explained Meshroom (AliceVision) open photogrammetry AliceVision the framework behind Meshroom MeshLab clean up and repair meshes Blender mesh editing Open or free-to-use tools and references picked by the author; links checked on 29 Oct 2026. chunks.title: Module 18: Applications and implications, project development | Fab Academy companion | Maker by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Individual assignment
chunks.text: Plan a final project masterpiece that integrates the range of units covered: what it will do, who has done what beforehand, what sources you will use, what you will design, what materials and components it needs, where they come from and what they cost, what parts and systems you will make, what processes you will use, what questions need answering, and how it will be evaluated. The project should incorporate 2D and 3D design, additive and subtractive fabrication, electronics design and production, embedded microcontroller design, interfacing and programming, and system integration and packaging. Where possible, make rather than buy the parts.

chunks.title: Module 18: Applications and implications, project development | Fab Academy companion | Maker by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Individual assignment
chunks.text: Projects can be separate or joint but need to show individual mastery and be independently operable. Project development: prepare drafts of your final project summary slide (presentation.png, 1920x1080) and video clip (presentation.mp4, 1080p).

chunks.heading: Learning outcomes

chunks.title: Module 18: Applications and implications, project development | Fab Academy companion | Maker by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Clarified in the official FAQ
chunks.text: The slide is presentation.png (1920x1080) and the video presentation.mp4 (1080p, about a minute, about 25 MB at most), both in the root of your site. All modules also follow the general essentials (original files in your archive, compressed media, acknowledgements, AI prompts documented) and the commercial board policy . Summary of both .

chunks.heading: Documentation checklist
chunks.text: The official "have you answered these questions?" list for this module, paraphrased. Tick each one off in your documentation. What will it do? Who has done what beforehand? What sources will you use? What will you design? What materials and components will you use, and where will they come from? How much will they cost? (a draft bill of materials is enough) What parts and systems will you make, and with what processes? What questions need answering, and how will it be evaluated? Uploaded a draft summary slide and video clip, and checked they are linked from the final presentation schedule.

chunks.text: For the group work, the minimum is to demonstrate a logic analyzer; other test equipment is welcome. Draw your board from scratch; modifying an existing EDA project does not count. A hand drawing is allowed, but you still have to show the use of EDA software. 'Interact and communicate' means a development board with local input and/or output, able to talk to an external device. chunks.title: Module 7: Electronics design | Fab Academy companion | Maker by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Bare-minimum
chunks.text: Group work: a documented observation of an embedded microcontroller using your lab's test equipment, with at least one photo or screenshot and a sentence on what it shows. State clearly what you did yourself. A schematic and a board layout made in an EDA tool, with the design files linked (source files, not only screenshots). Every part comes from your lab's inventory, and you list them (a simple bill of materials is enough). The design rules check was run against the rules for your fabrication process, and you show the result. A short explanation of what each important part of the circuit is for (power, programming header, reset, clock and the pins you used).

chunks.title: Module 7: Electronics design | Fab Academy companion | Maker by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Exceptional
chunks.text: Any of the official extras done properly: a simulated circuit with the results explained, a second design workflow compared with the first, or a case designed for the board. The board is designed for your final project, with decisions explained: alternatives you considered, datasheet references behind pin and power choices, and a rough power budget. Design rules tuned to your lab's actually characterized process rather than defaults, with the trace widths and clearances justified. Reproducible: custom footprints and libraries included, a BOM with part numbers, and a version history showing what the checks caught and what you changed.

chunks.heading: Bare-minimum
chunks.text: Group work: a comparison of the toolchains and workflows for at least two architectures, in your own words, with what you did and what differed in practice (setup, programming, debugging). Datasheet reading shown: name the microcontroller and quote the specific facts you used (pin functions, electrical limits, peripherals or registers) with the page or section. A program running on a microcontroller that both interacts with an input and/or output device and communicates over a wired or wireless link. The assignment names both, so show both. Evidence it works: the code in your repo, a photo or short video, and the serial or other output.

chunks.text: The official extras: the system assembled (running on a board you made) and more than one language or development environment tried, with an honest comparison. Going below the library: use timers, interrupts or registers directly where it matters, and show what you learned from the datasheet by doing it. A debugging story: something that failed, how you found the cause, and what you changed. Code that someone else can reuse: commented, with the exact build steps and versions, and files named clearly. A link to your final project: how this program becomes part of it. Ask the tutor about this module Coming back after a break?

chunks.title: Curriculum: what finished looks like, module by module | Maker by Curiosta
chunks.heading: General essentials
chunks.text: Keep your original, editable design files in your class archive (your GitLab repository), not on outside hosting. Talk to your instructor about any file over 10 MB; the final project video can be up to 25 MB. Compress images and video before you commit them. A 'hero shot' is a photo or video of the finished result. Acknowledge work by others, human or machine. If you used AI, document the prompts you used. Commercial boards follow the Commercial Board Policy: they are not evaluated as your own work. Documentation is in English. Students continuing from an earlier year are assessed against the current year's standards. Source: General essentials .

chunks.title: Curriculum: what finished looks like, module by module | Maker by Curiosta
chunks.heading: General essentials
chunks.text: Every student also signs the student agreement .

chunks.title: Curriculum: what finished looks like, module by module | Maker by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Commercial board policy
chunks.text: Commercial microcontroller boards are not evaluated as your design or production work. Arduino-type boards are accepted only as extra nodes, for example in networking, alongside a board you made. A single-board computer can stand in for a laptop (for example as the host for an interface). Source: Commercial board policy .

chunks.title: Curriculum: what finished looks like, module by module | Maker by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Midterm review
chunks.text: Documentation of the assignments so far is reviewed. Show progress on your final project idea and planning, with a system diagram, a task list and a schedule for the remaining work. Meet with your local and global instructors. Source: Midterm review .

chunks.title: Curriculum: what finished looks like, module by module | Maker by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Final project requirements
chunks.text: A summary slide (presentation.png, 1920x1080) and a roughly one-minute video (presentation.mp4, 1080p, up to about 25 MB) in the root of your site. A separate final project page, a bill of materials, links to the weeks that fed into it, how you did system integration, the licence you chose, and acknowledgements. Your own microcontroller PCB with an input and an output, 2D and 3D design, and additive and subtractive processes. A milled PCB counts as electronics production, not as the subtractive process. A shield for a commercial board does not meet the requirement, and a working tangle of wires is not enough integration. Source: Final project requirements .

chunks.text: Life happens. If you paused the course and want to pick it up again, here is a calm order of work. These steps are the author's suggestions for getting your bearings, not official Fab Academy policy. What your lab and instructor accept is their decision.

chunks.heading: Use the current cohort's pages
chunks.text: Fab Academy publishes its schedule and class pages per year. Assignments can change between years, so check the current year's pages on fabacademy.org before you rely on notes from an earlier cohort, including the dates and wording on this site, which come from the 2026 cohort.

chunks.title: Curriculum: what finished looks like, module by module | Maker by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Take stock of what you already have
chunks.text: Open your documentation site and repository and list, module by module, what exists and what is missing. Read each official assignment bullet on the module pages here and note which one has evidence and which does not.

chunks.title: Curriculum: what finished looks like, module by module | Maker by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Check your tools still work
chunks.text: Make sure you can still log in, commit and publish your documentation, and that your software and files open. Fix this first, because everything else depends on it.

chunks.title: Curriculum: what finished looks like, module by module | Maker by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Order the remaining work
chunks.text: As a suggestion (the author's, not an official rule): finish the modules that your final project depends on first. Electronics design, electronics production, input devices, output devices, networking and interface work build on each other, and system integration needs all of them.

chunks.title: Curriculum: what finished looks like, module by module | Maker by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Document the gap honestly
chunks.text: Say what you did and when, including the break. Your documentation is for readers who were not there, and an honest timeline is more useful to them than a tidy one.

chunks.title: Curriculum: what finished looks like, module by module | Maker by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Re-plan your final project
chunks.text: Read the final project requirements on the applications and implications page, and check that your plan still fits the time you have. Cutting scope early is better than cutting corners late. Ask the tutor where to start

chunks.heading: SDG 10 · Reduced Inequalities
chunks.text: Reduced Inequalities includes the inclusion of people regardless of disability, age or other status. Makers can co-design affordable, repairable assistive prototypes with users, testing with them rather than for them. 2 projects: Haptic Distance Wristband (ToF Sensor, Vibration Feedback); Laser-Cut Tactile Campus Map with Braille and Touch Audio Open SDG 10 · Reduced Inequalities →

chunks.title: Projects by goal | Maker by Curiosta
chunks.heading: SDG 11 · Sustainable Cities and Communities
chunks.text: This goal is about cities and communities that are inclusive, safe, resilient and sustainable, including lower environmental impact such as air quality and noise. Makers can build sensors that map local conditions and give neighbourhoods data to act on. 2 projects: Street Noise Level Meter (I2S Microphone, dB Logging); Bike-Mounted Road Quality and Pothole Mapper Open SDG 11 · Sustainable Cities and Communities →

chunks.title: Projects by goal | Maker by Curiosta
chunks.heading: SDG 12 · Responsible Consumption and Production
chunks.text: Responsible Consumption and Production asks us to use resources efficiently and cut waste through prevention, reduction, repair and recycling. Makers can build tools that support composting, repair and reuse, and design products to last. 2 projects: Compost Health Probe (Temperature + Moisture, Low-Power); PET-Bottle Strip Filament Pultruder Open SDG 12 · Responsible Consumption and Production →

chunks.title: Projects by goal | Maker by Curiosta
chunks.heading: SDG 13 · Climate Action
chunks.text: Climate Action covers urgent action on climate change and its impacts, including adaptation and awareness. Makers can build monitors that log local conditions such as heat and humidity over time, making local climate trends visible. 2 projects: ESP32 Climate Node: Heat-Index Monitor with OLED and MQTT Dashboard; Cool-Roof Experiment: Twin Laser-Cut Model Houses Open SDG 13 · Climate Action →

chunks.title: Projects by goal | Maker by Curiosta
chunks.heading: SDG 14 · Life Below Water
chunks.text: Life Below Water is about conserving oceans, seas and marine resources and reducing pollution that reaches them. Makers can build sensing buoys and loggers for lakes, rivers and coasts, testing carefully and leaving nothing behind in the water. 2 projects: LoRa Water-Quality Buoy (Temperature + Turbidity); Shoreline Microplastics Sieve Kit with Phone Microscope Stand Open SDG 14 · Life Below Water →

chunks.title: Projects by goal | Maker by Curiosta
chunks.heading: SDG 15 · Life on Land
chunks.text: Life on Land covers protecting forests, land ecosystems and biodiversity. Makers can support local biodiversity surveys with tools like camera traps, used with respect for wildlife, privacy and permission rules. 2 projects: PIR Wildlife Camera Trap (ESP32-CAM, 3D-Printed Housing); Acoustic Biodiversity Recorder (Scheduled Dawn Chorus Logger) Open SDG 15 · Life on Land →

chunks.title: Projects by goal | Maker by Curiosta
chunks.heading: SDG 16 · Peace, Justice and Strong Institutions
chunks.text: This goal aims for peaceful, inclusive societies with accountable institutions and participatory decision-making. Makers can explore designing for trust, transparency and fairness in small group processes such as club or classroom votes. 2 projects: Tamper-Evident Electronic Vote Box for Clubs and Classrooms; Tamper-Detecting Smart Seal (ATtiny, Cast in Epoxy) Open SDG 16 · Peace, Justice and Strong Institutions →

chunks.title: Projects by goal | Maker by Curiosta
chunks.heading: SDG 17 · Partnerships for the Goals
chunks.text: Partnerships for the Goals is about cooperation, technology sharing and open data across countries and sectors. Makers contribute by building to shared open standards, joining citizen-science networks and documenting their work so others can reuse it. 2 projects: Sensor.Community Air-Quality Node (Join a Global Open-Data Network); Twin-Lab LoRa Messenger (Build to a Shared Open Spec) Open SDG 17 · Partnerships for the Goals →
